topics.title: REST API Design
topics.summary: Model resources as nouns, use HTTP methods for actions, and keep responses and errors consistent.
topics.description:
**REST** is a set of conventions for building HTTP APIs around **resources** (things such as users, orders, products).

### URLs are nouns, methods are verbs
| Method | URL | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/v1/users` | list users |
| GET | `/api/v1/users/42` | read one user |
| POST | `/api/v1/users` | create a user |
| PUT | `/api/v1/users/42` | replace a user |
| PATCH | `/api/v1/users/42` | partially update |
| DELETE | `/api/v1/users/42` | delete |

### Design rules
* Use plural nouns and nesting only for ownership: `/users/42/orders`.
* **Version** the API (`/api/v1`) so you can evolve it.
* **Filter, sort, paginate** with query strings: `?status=paid&sort=-createdAt&page=2&limit=20`.
* Return JSON with a consistent envelope and **proper status codes** (see the HTTP status codes topic).
* **Idempotency**: GET, PUT, DELETE can be repeated safely; POST usually cannot.
* Validate input on the server and return field-level error messages.
* Protect with authentication, rate limiting and CORS rules.

### Error format
Pick one shape and use it everywhere: `{ "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "Email is invalid", "fields": { "email": "invalid" } } }`.
keyPoints: Resources are nouns, HTTP methods are the verbs
Version your API from day one
Use query params for filter/sort/pagination
Return correct status codes and a consistent error shape
GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent
pitfalls: Always returning 200 with an error message in the body

examples.title: Express route skeleton
examples.code:
app.get('/api/v1/users', listUsers);        // GET collection
app.get('/api/v1/users/:id', getUser);       // GET one
app.post('/api/v1/users', createUser);       // POST -> 201 Created
app.patch('/api/v1/users/:id', updateUser);  // PATCH -> 200
app.delete('/api/v1/users/:id', deleteUser); // DELETE -> 204 No Content
examples.explanation: One resource, five routes, conventional methods.

interview.a: `PUT` replaces the whole resource; `PATCH` changes only the supplied fields.
Making the same request several times has the same effect as making it once (e.g. DELETE /users/42).
Offset (`page`/`limit`) is simple; cursor-based pagination scales better for large or changing data sets.

topics.title: HTTP Status Codes
topics.summary: The code families (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx) and the specific codes an API should return.
topics.description:
A status code tells the client **what happened** before it even reads the body.

### Families
| Range | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1xx | informational |
| 2xx | success |
| 3xx | redirection |
| 4xx | **client** error - the request is wrong |
| 5xx | **server** error - we failed |

### Codes you must know
* **200 OK** - request succeeded.
* **201 Created** - a resource was created (POST).
* **204 No Content** - success, nothing to return (DELETE).
* **301 / 302** - permanent / temporary redirect; **304 Not Modified** - use your cache.
* **400 Bad Request** - malformed or invalid input.
* **401 Unauthorized** - not authenticated (no or bad credentials).
* **403 Forbidden** - authenticated but not allowed.
* **404 Not Found** - resource does not exist.
* **409 Conflict** - state conflict (duplicate email, edit conflict).
* **422 Unprocessable Entity** - validation errors on well-formed input.
* **429 Too Many Requests** - rate limit hit (send `Retry-After`).
* **500 Internal Server Error** - unexpected bug; **502/503/504** - bad gateway, unavailable, gateway timeout.

### 401 vs 403
**401** = "who are you?" (log in). **403** = "I know who you are, but you may not do this."
keyPoints: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
201 for create, 204 for empty success
401 = not logged in, 403 = not allowed
429 signals rate limiting
Never leak stack traces in 500 responses

examples.title: Express handlers
examples.code:
res.status(201).json(newUser);                       // created
res.status(204).end();                              // deleted
res.status(400).json({ error: 'Email required' });  // bad input
res.status(401).json({ error: 'Login required' });  // no/invalid token
res.status(403).json({ error: 'Admins only' });     // forbidden
res.status(404).json({ error: 'User not found' });  // missing
res.status(429).json({ error: 'Slow down' });       // rate limit
examples.explanation: Choose the code that describes the outcome precisely.

interview.a: 400 for syntactically bad requests, 422 for well-formed requests that fail semantic validation (many teams use 400 for both).

topics.title: Authentication: Sessions, JWT & OAuth
topics.summary: How sessions, JSON Web Tokens and OAuth 2.0 differ, and when to use each.
topics.description:
**Authentication** answers "who are you?"; **authorization** answers "what may you do?".

### Session (stateful)
The server stores the session (in memory, DB or Redis) and sends the browser a **session id cookie**. Every request looks the session up. Easy to revoke, but needs shared storage when you run many servers (Redis!).

### JWT (stateless)
A signed token `header.payload.signature` holding claims (user id, role, expiry). The server only verifies the signature - no lookup needed, so it scales across servers easily. Downsides: hard to revoke before expiry, payload is only encoded (not encrypted).

* Keep **access tokens short-lived** (about 15 minutes) and use a **refresh token** (stored in an httpOnly cookie, rotated) to get new ones.
* Never put secrets in the payload.

### OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect
A protocol to **delegate** login to a provider ("Sign in with Google"). Your app never sees the user's password; it receives an authorization code, exchanges it for tokens. OAuth is about authorization; **OIDC** adds identity on top.

### Storage in the browser
Prefer **httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies** (not readable by JavaScript, safer against XSS). Hash passwords with **bcrypt/argon2**, always use HTTPS.
keyPoints: Session = server remembers you, JWT = token proves you
JWT is signed, not encrypted
Short access token + refresh token
OAuth delegates login to a provider
Hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2; use HTTPS and httpOnly cookies
pitfalls: Long-lived JWTs that cannot be revoked
Putting sensitive data in a JWT payload

examples.title: JWT with Express (sketch)
examples.explanation: Sign on login, verify on every protected request.

examples.title: JWT structure
examples.code:
xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz
  |     |     |
header payload signature
(alg)  (claims) HMAC(header+payload, secret)
examples.explanation: Anyone can read the payload (base64); only the server can create a valid signature.

interview.a: Sessions keep state on the server and are easy to revoke; JWTs are self-contained, stateless and scale well but are harder to revoke.
Authentication verifies identity; authorization decides what that identity may do.
So access tokens can be short-lived (limiting damage if stolen) without forcing users to log in again.

topics.title: Caching Basics
topics.summary: Store expensive results closer to the user so requests skip slow work: browser, CDN, application and database caches.
topics.description:
A **cache** keeps a copy of data that is expensive to compute or fetch so the next request is fast. It reduces latency **and** protects your database.

### Layers
1. **Browser cache** - controlled with `Cache-Control`, `ETag`.
2. **CDN** - static assets and even API responses served from edge locations near users.
3. **Application cache** - in-memory or **Redis**: query results, rendered fragments, sessions.
4. **Database cache** - buffer pool, query cache.

### Strategies
* **Cache-aside (lazy loading)**: read cache; on miss read DB and store in cache. Most common.
* **Write-through**: write to cache and DB together.
* **Write-back**: write to cache, flush to DB later (fast, risk of loss).

### Expiry & invalidation
Use a **TTL** (time to live) and **invalidate** keys when the data changes. "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."

### Problems to know
* **Stale data** - users see old values until TTL expires.
* **Cache stampede** - many requests rebuild an expired hot key simultaneously; use locks or jittered TTLs.
* **Eviction** - when memory is full (LRU is the usual policy).
keyPoints: Cache-aside: check cache, fall back to DB, then fill cache
Always set a TTL
Invalidate on write
Hot keys can cause a stampede
Measure the hit ratio
pitfalls: Caching user-specific data under a shared key
No TTL leading to permanently stale data
Caching before optimising slow queries or missing indexes

examples.title: Cache-aside with Redis
examples.explanation: The classic read path; remember to delete the key when the product is updated.

interview.a: The application checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss and writes the value into the cache.
Many simultaneous requests miss an expired popular key and all hit the database at once; mitigate with locking, request coalescing or staggered TTLs.

topics.title: Database Indexing
topics.summary: An index is a sorted lookup structure that turns full-table scans into fast seeks - at the cost of slower writes.
topics.description:
Without an index the database must read **every row** (a *full table scan*) to find matches. An **index** is an extra data structure (usually a **B-tree**) that keeps column values sorted with pointers to rows, like the index at the back of a book.

### When indexes help
* Columns in `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `ORDER BY`.
* Foreign keys.
* Columns with high **selectivity** (many distinct values, e.g. email) - not a boolean flag.

### Types
* **Primary / unique** index - enforces uniqueness.
* **Composite** index `(user_id, created_at)` - follows the **leftmost prefix** rule: it helps queries filtering by `user_id` or `user_id + created_at`, but not by `created_at` alone.
* **Partial**, **full-text**, **hash**, **covering** indexes for special cases.

### Costs
Every index uses disk/memory and slows `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` because it must be updated. Index what you query, not everything.

### Verify with EXPLAIN
Run `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) to see whether the planner uses an index (Index Scan) or reads everything (Seq Scan).

In scaling terms indexing is the **first** thing to do before caching or sharding.
keyPoints: Index = sorted structure (B-tree) for fast lookup
Index columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY
Composite indexes obey the leftmost-prefix rule
Indexes slow writes and use space
Check plans with EXPLAIN
pitfalls: Functions on the column (`WHERE LOWER(email)=...`) bypassing the index
Wrong column order in a composite index

examples.title: Create and verify an index
examples.explanation: One composite index serves both the filter and the sort.

examples.title: MongoDB equivalent
examples.code:
db.orders.createIndex({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
db.orders.find({ userId: 42 }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).explain('executionStats');
examples.explanation: Same idea in a document database.

interview.a: Indexes consume space and make every write slower because each index has to be maintained.

interview.q: What is the leftmost prefix rule?
interview.a: A composite index can be used only for queries that filter on its first column(s) in order.

topics.title: SQL vs NoSQL
topics.summary: Relational databases favour structure and transactions; NoSQL stores trade some of that for flexibility and horizontal scale.
topics.description:
### SQL (relational) - PostgreSQL, MySQL
* Data in **tables** with a fixed schema; relations via foreign keys and **JOINs**.
* Strong **ACID** transactions (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable).
* Powerful queries (aggregations, joins).
* Scales vertically first; horizontal scaling (replicas, sharding) takes more effort.

### NoSQL
| Type | Example | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Document | MongoDB | flexible JSON-like records, content, catalogs |
| Key-value | Redis, DynamoDB | cache, sessions, counters |
| Wide-column | Cassandra | huge write-heavy time series |
| Graph | Neo4j | relationships, recommendations |
| Search | Elasticsearch | full-text search |

* Flexible/evolving schema, designed for horizontal scaling.
* Often **eventual consistency** (BASE) and weaker joins - you model data around your queries and may duplicate data.

### How to choose
* Money, orders, inventory, anything relational -> **SQL**.
* Rapidly changing shape, hierarchical documents, massive scale -> **NoSQL**.
* Real systems are **polyglot**: PostgreSQL as the source of truth, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search.
keyPoints: SQL: schema, joins, ACID transactions
NoSQL: flexible schema, horizontal scale, eventual consistency
Pick by access patterns, not by trend
Polyglot persistence is normal in big systems
pitfalls: Choosing NoSQL just to "avoid schemas" and ending up with an implicit one
Forcing highly relational data into a document store

examples.title: Same data, two models
examples.explanation: SQL joins at read time; documents pre-join by embedding.

interview.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - the guarantees of a database transaction.
For flexible, document-shaped data that is read as a whole and when the schema changes often or needs easy horizontal scaling.
